stimulus.description: A table listing five Texas cities and towns, the part of Texas where each is located, and where each place name came from.
stimulus.source: Handbook of Texas Online, Texas State Historical Association, entries for Nacogdoches, San Antonio, El Paso, New Braunfels, and Fredericksburg (accessed November 8, 2026)

practice.stem: Which conclusion is best supported by the place names in the table?

options.A: German settlers were the first group to name places in East Texas.
options.B: Spanish place names are found mainly in the Hill Country of central Texas.
options.C: Indigenous place names disappeared from Texas after Spanish colonization.
options.D: Place names record the groups that lived in or settled Texas over time.
options.E: Most Texas place names came from English through contagious diffusion.

practice.explanation: A toponym is a place name. Place names are like a history book written on the map. Nacogdoches comes from a Caddo people. San Antonio and El Paso come from Spanish explorers and settlers. New Braunfels and Fredericksburg come from German immigrants. Each group left its language on the land. Your AP course guide says toponyms can show how languages diffused.

whyNot.A: Nacogdoches, in East Texas, comes from a Caddo people, not from German settlers.
whyNot.B: The two Spanish names shown are in south-central and far western Texas. Five examples cannot show where most Spanish place names are.
whyNot.C: Nacogdoches shows that Indigenous names are still on the map.
whyNot.E: The table gives Indigenous, Spanish, and German naming histories. It does not support a claim about most Texas place names or show contagious diffusion of English.

practice.stem: Which pairing correctly describes one of the hypotheses proposed for the early spread of the Indo-European language family?

options.A: Kurgan hypothesis: the family spread with early farmers moving out of present-day Türkiye
options.B: Anatolian hypothesis: the family spread with the diffusion of farming from present-day Türkiye
options.C: Anatolian hypothesis: the family spread with horse-riding herders from the Eurasian steppe
options.D: Kurgan hypothesis: the family spread with traders from the Arabian Peninsula
options.E: Anatolian hypothesis: the family spread from China along the Silk Roads

practice.explanation: Indo-European is the language family with the most speakers today. It includes English, Spanish, Hindi, and Russian. Two well-known ideas link its early spread to people moving. The Anatolian hypothesis ties it to farming, which spread out of Anatolia (in today's Türkiye). The steppe, or Kurgan, hypothesis ties a later spread to herders from the grasslands north of the Black and Caspian Seas. Researchers keep testing both ideas.

whyNot.A: That swaps the two. The Kurgan hypothesis is about horse-riding herders from the steppe.
whyNot.C: That swaps the two. The Anatolian hypothesis is about farming spreading from Anatolia, in present-day Türkiye.
whyNot.D: Neither hypothesis puts the hearth on the Arabian Peninsula. Arabic, spoken there, belongs to a different family (Afro-Asiatic).
whyNot.E: Neither hypothesis puts the hearth in China. Chinese languages belong to a different family (Sino-Tibetan).

practice.stem: Malagasy, the main language of Madagascar, an island off the southeastern coast of Africa, belongs to the Austronesian language family. Its closest relatives are languages spoken on the island of Borneo in Southeast Asia, thousands of kilometers away. Which process best explains this pattern?

options.A: Contagious diffusion through neighboring areas of the African mainland
options.B: Hierarchical diffusion from colonial capitals in Europe
options.C: Stimulus diffusion of an African language that was later rewritten
options.D: Creolization of French and Arabic during the colonial period
options.E: Relocation diffusion by settlers who crossed the Indian Ocean by boat

practice.explanation: Relocation diffusion happens when people move and carry their culture to a new place. Malagasy's closest relatives are spoken on Borneo. That points to people who sailed across the Indian Ocean many centuries ago. They brought their language to Madagascar. There it kept changing through contact with other languages.

whyNot.A: Spread from nearby mainland communities would not explain why Malagasy's closest relatives are languages of Borneo.
whyNot.B: Madagascar was a French colony, but French is Indo-European. Colonial rule does not explain an Austronesian language.
whyNot.C: Changes in writing do not move a language into a different language family.
whyNot.D: Malagasy is not a mix of French and Arabic. It is related to languages of Borneo.

practice.stem: Which characteristic most helps explain why universalizing religions such as Christianity, Islam, and Buddhism have spread over much larger areas than ethnic religions such as Hinduism and Judaism?

options.A: They are much older than ethnic religions, so they had more time to spread.
options.B: They seek followers from all cultures and actively welcome new converts.
options.C: Their beliefs are closely tied to the land and people of their hearth.
options.D: They spread mainly when their followers migrated, rather than by converting others.
options.E: Their followers are concentrated in the region where the religion began.

practice.explanation: Universalizing religions teach that their message is open to people of any background. Winning new believers helps them spread to many cultures. Migration and trade help too. Ethnic religions usually have strong ties to one people, history, and place. They may still accept converts and spread when their followers move.

whyNot.A: Hinduism and Judaism are older than Christianity, Islam, and Buddhism, so age does not explain it.
whyNot.C: Strong ties to the land and people of the hearth are more typical of ethnic religions.
whyNot.D: Universalizing religions spread through conversion (expansion diffusion) as well as migration (relocation diffusion).
whyNot.E: Staying near the hearth does not explain spread across many cultures. Some ethnic religions have communities far from their hearths, and some universalizing religions stay mostly in one region.

practice.stem: Sikhism began in the Punjab region of South Asia in the late 1400s and early 1500s. Today large Sikh communities, with gurdwaras (Sikh houses of worship), are found in places such as Surrey in Canada, Southall in London, and Yuba City in California. These communities are best explained by

options.A: contagious diffusion from Punjab into neighboring regions of Europe
options.B: hierarchical diffusion, as the faith reached the world's largest cities first and then smaller towns
options.C: relocation diffusion, as Sikhs migrated from Punjab and brought their faith
options.D: stimulus diffusion, as local churches adopted and changed Sikh beliefs
options.E: expansion diffusion, as many local residents in these places converted to Sikhism

practice.explanation: Families from Punjab moved to these cities. They built gurdwaras and kept practicing their faith. When people carry their religion to a new place by moving there, that is relocation diffusion. A universalizing religion like Sikhism can spread by people moving, not only by people converting.

whyNot.A: Punjab and Europe are not neighbors. The faith jumped long distances with people who moved.
whyNot.B: The communities formed where Sikh families settled for work, including small Yuba City, not in order of city size.
whyNot.D: Stimulus diffusion means an idea spreads but changes form. Here Sikhs themselves moved and kept their religion.
whyNot.E: The communities grew mainly because Sikh families moved there, not because many local residents converted.

practice.stem: Which of the following best distinguishes acculturation from assimilation?

options.A: Acculturation affects immigrants, while assimilation affects the host society that receives them.
options.B: Acculturation blends two religions into one, while assimilation blends two languages into one.
options.C: Acculturation happens at the global scale, while assimilation happens at the local scale.
options.D: Acculturation adds some new traits, while assimilation means largely merging into the main culture
options.E: Acculturation keeps cultures fully separate, while assimilation lets them coexist as equals.

practice.explanation: Acculturation means picking up some new traits from another culture while keeping parts of your own. Assimilation means becoming more like the main culture around you. People who assimilate often use some of their old traditions less. These changes can be uneven. A family may switch languages but keep its holiday traditions.

whyNot.A: Both terms usually describe changes in a newcomer or minority group. The difference is how much of the original culture is kept.
whyNot.B: Religious blending is syncretism. Creolization can produce a new community language through long language contact. Neither one defines acculturation or assimilation.
whyNot.C: Both can happen at any scale. Scale is not what separates them.
whyNot.E: Acculturation happens through contact and borrowing, so it does not keep cultures fully separate. Groups living side by side while keeping their identities is multiculturalism, not assimilation.

stimulus.title: LANGUAGE AND TRADITIONS AMONG FAMILIES FROM COUNTRY F LIVING IN COUNTRY G (HYPOTHETICAL DATA)
columns: Speak Country G's main language well (%)
Celebrate Country F's New Year festival (%)
stimulus.description: A table comparing three generations of families from Country F living in Country G: the percent who speak Language F at home, the percent who speak Country G's main language well, and the percent who celebrate Country F's New Year festival.

practice.stem: Which conclusion is best supported by the data in the table?

options.A: The data suggest growing linguistic assimilation alongside continued heritage traditions.
options.B: Most members of the third generation no longer celebrate the New Year festival.
options.C: The data show syncretism, because the families have blended two religions into one.
options.D: The first generation has fully assimilated, since 92 percent of them speak Language F.
options.E: Each generation keeps its heritage language as strongly as the generation before it.

practice.explanation: Read down each column. Fewer people in each generation speak Language F at home. More of them speak Country G's language well. That fits linguistic assimilation, which means shifting toward the main language. But 52% of the grandchildren still celebrate the festival. So the table does not show that the heritage culture is gone.

whyNot.B: 52% of the third generation still celebrate the festival. That is more than half.
whyNot.C: The table has no data about religion, so it cannot show religions blending.
whyNot.D: Speaking Language F at home does not show full assimilation into Country G's culture. It shows that the heritage language is still being used.
whyNot.E: Speaking Language F at home falls in each generation, from 92% to 55% to 14%.

practice.stem: In Mexico, Día de los Muertos (Day of the Dead) falls on November 1 and 2, the dates of the Catholic holy days of All Saints' Day and All Souls' Day. Families build altars with marigolds, candles, food, and photos to honor relatives who have died, customs that many scholars trace to Indigenous Mesoamerican traditions. This celebration best illustrates

options.A: syncretism
options.B: assimilation
options.C: multiculturalism
options.D: ethnocentrism
options.E: relocation diffusion

practice.explanation: Syncretism is the blending of two or more cultural traditions into something new. Many scholars see Day of the Dead as a mix of Catholic holy days, brought by the Spanish, and older Indigenous ways of honoring ancestors. Neither tradition simply replaced the other. They merged.

whyNot.B: Assimilation means adopting a dominant culture. This example describes two traditions combining into one celebration.
whyNot.C: Multiculturalism recognizes several cultural groups and their identities. This question is about traditions blending together, which is syncretism.
whyNot.D: Ethnocentrism is judging other cultures by one's own standards. It does not describe this blending.
whyNot.E: Relocation diffusion is spread by people moving. The key idea here is two traditions blending in one place.

practice.stem: English speakers in the southern United States, New England, and the Upper Midwest can understand one another, but they differ in pronunciation and in some everyday words. For example, a soft drink is often called "soda" in New England, "pop" in much of the Midwest, and "coke" in much of the South. These regional varieties of English are best described as

options.A: separate language families
options.B: pidgins
options.C: dialects
options.D: lingua francas
options.E: language isolates

practice.explanation: A dialect is a regional or social version of one language. Speakers of different dialects can usually understand each other, but they use different sounds, words, or grammar. "Soda," "pop," and "coke" are a classic example in American English. A line on a map that marks where one word or sound stops and another starts is called an isogloss.

whyNot.A: A language family is a group of related languages. These are all varieties of one language, English.
whyNot.B: A pidgin is a contact language for people who share no language. These speakers all speak English.
whyNot.D: A lingua franca is a shared language used by people with different first languages. Here everyone already shares English.
whyNot.E: A language isolate has no known relatives, like Basque. English belongs to the Indo-European family.

stimulus.title: LANGUAGE SPOKEN AT HOME, BY REGION, COUNTRY H (HYPOTHETICAL DATA)
stimulus.description: A table showing, for each of four regions of Country H and for the country as a whole, the region's share of the national population and the percent of people who speak Language A or Language B at home.

practice.stem: A national report on Country H states, "Only 15 percent of people speak Language B at home, so language is unlikely to divide the country." Based on the table, which statement best explains a weakness in this conclusion?

options.A: The regional percentages add up to more than 100, so the national figure is wrong.
options.B: Language B is spoken by so few people that it cannot shape any region's identity.
options.C: The conclusion should use global-scale data, since languages cross national borders.
options.D: Language B is spreading quickly, so it will soon be the national majority language.
options.E: The national figure hides that Language B speakers are a large majority in the East region.

practice.explanation: The national number, 15%, is an average for the whole country. Zoom in to the regional scale, and the picture changes: 82% of people in the East speak Language B at home. A group that is small nationally but a large majority in one region can have a strong regional identity, which can become a centrifugal force. Changing the scale of analysis can change the conclusion.

whyNot.A: In each row, Language A and Language B add to 100%, and the regions' population shares add to 100%. The 15% national figure matches the regional data.
whyNot.B: In the East, 82% speak Language B at home, so it clearly can shape that region's identity.
whyNot.C: The question is about unity inside Country H. Regional data, not global data, show where Language B speakers are concentrated.
whyNot.D: The table shows one point in time, so it gives no evidence about how fast Language B is spreading.

practice.stem: Rail systems in several large cities, including Tokyo, Mexico City, and Delhi, set aside some train cars for women only. In the 2000s, rail companies in Tokyo added women-only cars in response to complaints about the harassment of women on crowded trains. This policy best illustrates how

options.A: time-space convergence has made rush-hour trains much less crowded
options.B: religious laws in these cities require men and women to stay apart in public spaces
options.C: fewer women now ride public transportation to get to work
options.D: concerns about gender and safety can shape how public space is designed and used
options.E: cultural relativism can lead cities to copy one another's transit systems

practice.explanation: Your AP course guide says attitudes about gender help shape how people use space. Many women ride crowded trains to work and school. Because of concerns about harassment, some cities reserve cars for women. That changes how a public space is designed and used.

whyNot.A: The policy exists because trains are crowded, not because they have become less crowded.
whyNot.B: The question describes a safety measure on crowded trains, not a religious law. Men and women share most public spaces in these cities.
whyNot.C: Women-only cars make sense where many women ride trains, so the policy points to heavy use by women, not less.
whyNot.E: Cultural relativism is an attitude toward other cultures. It does not explain this safety policy.

exam.title: Unit 3 Practice Exam: Cultural Patterns and Processes
exam.directions: Each of the questions or incomplete statements below is followed by five suggested answers or completions. Select the one that is best in each case. Your score is based only on the number of questions answered correctly, so answer every question. Work quickly without losing accuracy, and come back to any question you skipped if time allows.

questions.stem: Friday-night high school football games, tailgating, marching bands, homecoming mums, and school colors are related traits that together form a

options.A: culture region
options.B: cultural hearth
options.C: culture complex
options.D: culture trait
options.E: cultural landscape

rationales.A: Incorrect. A culture region is an area in which people share particular culture traits; the question describes a set of related traits, not an area.
rationales.B: Incorrect. A cultural hearth is the place where a culture trait or culture originated.
rationales.C: Correct. A culture complex is a group of related culture traits that together make up a larger cultural activity, such as the practices connected to high school football.
rationales.D: Incorrect. A culture trait is a single attribute of a culture; the question lists several related traits that function together.
rationales.E: Incorrect. The cultural landscape is the visible imprint of culture on a place, such as a stadium. Tailgating, bands, and school colors together are better described as a complex of related traits.

questions.explanation: One trait is one piece of culture, like wearing school colors. A culture complex is a group of related traits that go together. Football games, tailgating, marching bands, homecoming mums, and school colors all connect to one activity, so together they form a culture complex.

questions.stem: A tourist complains that people in the country she is visiting eat with their hands instead of with forks, and she calls the local way of eating uncivilized. Her attitude is an example of

options.A: acculturation
options.B: cultural relativism
options.C: ethnocentrism
options.D: syncretism
options.E: cultural convergence

rationales.A: Incorrect. Acculturation is the adoption of some traits of another culture; the tourist rejects the local practice rather than adopting it.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Cultural relativism is the opposite attitude: evaluating a culture's practices on their own terms rather than by an outside standard.
rationales.C: Correct. Ethnocentrism is the attitude that one's own culture is superior and the use of one's own cultural standards to judge other cultures.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Syncretism is the blending of traits from different cultures into a new form.
rationales.E: Incorrect. Cultural convergence is the process by which cultures become more alike through contact.

questions.explanation: Ethnocentrism means judging another culture by your own culture's rules. It means deciding that your way is better. In many cultures, eating with your hands is normal and polite. Calling it "uncivilized" just because it is different from home is ethnocentric.

questions.setLabel: Questions 3–5 refer to the map below.

stimulus.title: SPREAD OF A NEW MUSIC STYLE IN COUNTRY R, 2010–2016 (HYPOTHETICAL)
stimulus.description: Circles show cities and towns in Country R; larger circles mean more people. Each label gives the place's name, its population, and the year the music style first became popular there. The style began in Arlo, the hearth. Fenn is about 120 kilometers from Arlo; Benn and Cora are each more than 450 kilometers from Arlo.
stimulus.renderNotes: One land polygon for Country R on a water background. City circles (island features) sized by population, each with a one-line label underneath. Scale bar bottom left: 100 px = 100 km.

questions.stem: The order of adoption shown on the map is most consistent with which type of diffusion?

options.A: Contagious diffusion
options.B: Relocation diffusion
options.C: Stimulus diffusion
options.D: Hierarchical diffusion
options.E: Reverse hierarchical diffusion

rationales.A: Incorrect. Contagious diffusion would reach the places nearest the hearth first. Fenn, only about 120 kilometers from Arlo, adopted the style in 2015, years after much more distant large cities.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The map does not show migration. Its clearest pattern is that larger cities adopted the style before smaller places.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Stimulus diffusion involves an underlying idea spreading while the trait itself is changed; the map gives no evidence that the style changed.
rationales.D: Correct. Distant large cities adopted the style before nearby small towns. This sequence fits diffusion down an urban hierarchy better than a spread organized mainly by distance.
rationales.E: Incorrect. Reverse hierarchical diffusion moves from small places up to larger ones; here the smallest places adopted the style last.

questions.explanation: Follow the years. Arlo, the biggest city, had it in 2010. The big cities Benn and Cora got it in 2011. The medium cities Dell and Eskar got it in 2013. The small towns Fenn and Gale got it last, in 2015 and 2016. The style moved down the ladder of city size, not outward by distance. That is hierarchical diffusion.

questions.stem: Which explanation best accounts for Fenn's adoption date compared with those of Benn and Cora?

options.A: Distance decay means places nearest a hearth tend to be the last to adopt a trait.
options.B: The style reached Fenn when people from Arlo moved there, through relocation diffusion.
options.C: New trends often move first between big, well-connected cities, then down to small towns.
options.D: Fenn's small population places it in a different culture region from the rest of Country R.
options.E: Contagious diffusion spreads a trait to the largest places first and the closest places last.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Distance decay means interaction declines as distance increases, so nearby places usually adopt a trait sooner, not later.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The map contains no migration history, so this explanation is not supported by the evidence provided.
rationales.C: Correct. In hierarchical diffusion, a trait moves first among the largest and most connected places, through media, business, and travel links, and reaches small towns later, even towns close to the hearth.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Nothing on the map suggests Fenn belongs to a different culture region; Fenn and Gale, the two smallest places, both adopted the style last, which reflects their size.
rationales.E: Incorrect. This misdefines contagious diffusion, which spreads to the nearest people and places first regardless of size.

questions.explanation: Big cities are tied to each other by media companies, concert tours, airports, and lots of travelers. So a new trend jumps from one big city to another first. Small towns get it later, even if they are close by. That is why little Fenn waited until 2015.

questions.stem: Assume that use of streaming services and social media became much more widespread throughout Country R after 2016. If another music style first appeared in Arlo in 2024, its spread, compared with the pattern on the map, would most likely be

options.A: slower, because online media make distance decay stronger
options.B: limited mainly to large cities, because small towns lack media companies
options.C: about the same, because trends would still move down the urban hierarchy year by year
options.D: carried mainly by migrants, making relocation diffusion the main process
options.E: faster and less tied to city size, because of time-space convergence

rationales.A: Incorrect. Online media weaken the effect of distance on interaction; they do not strengthen distance decay.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Listeners do not need local media companies to stream music; anyone with internet access can hear a new style, wherever they live.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The AP course framework notes that communication technologies such as the internet are reshaping and accelerating interactions among people, so the slow, year-by-year movement down the urban hierarchy shown on the map would be much less likely.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Online sharing spreads a trait without people moving, so relocation diffusion would not become the main process.
rationales.E: Correct. Time-space convergence, the shrinking of the time it takes for people and ideas to travel between places, means people in small towns can hear a new style online at nearly the same time as people in big cities. Adoption would be faster and depend less on the urban hierarchy.

questions.explanation: When almost everyone can stream music, people in small towns can hear a new style at nearly the same time as people in big cities. That can shrink the delays caused by distance and city size. (Hearing a style does not guarantee that people will adopt it.) This is time-space convergence at work.

questions.stem: In the early 1800s, Sequoyah, a Cherokee man who did not read English, saw that English speakers could communicate through writing. He then created a new writing system, with a symbol for each syllable of the Cherokee language, which he completed in 1821. This is an example of

options.A: stimulus diffusion
options.B: relocation diffusion
options.C: contagious diffusion
options.D: hierarchical diffusion
options.E: assimilation

rationales.A: Correct. In stimulus diffusion, an underlying idea spreads, but the trait itself is changed or reinvented by the receiving culture. The idea of writing spread, and Sequoyah created a new system for the Cherokee language rather than adopting English writing.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The example emphasizes how an idea was adapted, rather than the movement of people who carried a trait.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Person-to-person spread alone does not describe the central feature here: adapting the idea of writing into a different writing system.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Hierarchical diffusion moves from people or places of high rank down the hierarchy; the key feature here is the transformation of the idea.
rationales.E: Incorrect. The syllabary supported the use of the Cherokee language rather than its replacement by English.

questions.explanation: Stimulus diffusion means the IDEA spreads, but people change it to fit their own culture. Sequoyah got the idea of writing from seeing English, but he made a brand-new writing system for Cherokee.

questions.stem: A pilot whose first language is Portuguese and an air traffic controller whose first language is Japanese use English to communicate during an international flight. English in this interaction is best described as

options.A: a creole
options.B: a lingua franca
options.C: a dialect
options.D: a language isolate
options.E: a pidgin

rationales.A: Incorrect. A creole develops in a language-contact setting and is spoken as a first language by a community. This example describes people using an existing language to communicate across language differences.
rationales.B: Correct. A lingua franca is a language used for communication among people who do not share a first language. English plays this role in international aviation, as well as in much of international business and science.
rationales.C: Incorrect. A dialect is a regional or social variety of a language.
rationales.D: Incorrect. A language isolate has no known relationship to other languages, as with Basque; English belongs to the Germanic branch of the Indo-European family.
rationales.E: Incorrect. A pidgin develops for limited communication among groups without a shared language. Aviation English is a specialized use of English, not a separate pidgin language.

questions.explanation: A lingua franca is a "bridge" language that people use when they do not share a first language. The pilot speaks Portuguese and the controller speaks Japanese, but both can use English. In international aviation, English often plays this role.

questions.stem: Portuguese is an official language in Brazil, Angola, Mozambique, and Timor-Leste, countries on three different continents. Which of the following best explains this pattern?

options.A: Portuguese spread by contagious diffusion from Brazil to Africa and then to Asia.
options.B: The four countries joined an international organization that made Portuguese their shared official language.
options.C: Portuguese formed as a pidgin among traders in Africa and later spread to Europe.
options.D: Large numbers of Portuguese workers moved to these countries during the last 20 years.
options.E: Portugal colonized these places, and each kept or restored Portuguese as an official language.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Contagious diffusion spreads to nearby places; these countries are separated by oceans, and Portuguese reached each one by sea from Portugal.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The Community of Portuguese Language Countries, founded in 1996, brought together countries that already used Portuguese; the shared language came first, from colonial rule.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Portuguese is a Romance language that developed in Europe from Latin; it did not begin as an African trade pidgin.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Some Portuguese did move to Angola and Brazil recently, but Portuguese was official there long before that, and recent migration cannot explain centuries of use in all four countries.
rationales.E: Correct. Portuguese colonial rule spread the language through administration, education, religion, and trade. After independence, these states kept Portuguese as an official language or, in Timor-Leste's case, restored it after a period of Indonesian occupation.

questions.explanation: These countries are far apart, but all were once ruled by Portugal. That history shaped their later choices of official language. Today Portuguese is official in all four, alongside Tetum in Timor-Leste.

questions.stem: Haitian Creole developed in the 1600s and 1700s in the French colony of Saint-Domingue (present-day Haiti), among French colonists and enslaved Africans who spoke many different African languages. Much of its vocabulary comes from French, but it has its own grammar. Today it is the first language of most Haitians. The development of Haitian Creole best illustrates

options.A: language extinction caused by the spread of a colonial language
options.B: creolization resulting from contact between cultures under colonialism
options.C: the diffusion of an Indo-European language by contagious expansion
options.D: stimulus diffusion of the idea of writing from West Africa to Europe
options.E: the formation of a dialect through isolation from other languages

rationales.A: Incorrect. The passage describes the emergence of Haitian Creole. It does not establish that another language became extinct.
rationales.B: Correct. Contact among French-speaking colonists and enslaved speakers of different African languages contributed to the emergence of a new language. This is an example of creolization in a colonial setting.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Haitian Creole formed through intense contact among groups within one colony, not through the gradual spread of French into neighboring areas.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The question describes a new spoken language forming, not the spread of the idea of writing.
rationales.E: Incorrect. Haitian Creole formed through contact among speakers of different languages, the opposite of isolation.

questions.explanation: Haitian Creole grew out of contact among people who spoke different languages under French colonial rule. It developed its own patterns and rules, and children learned it as their first language. That is creolization.

questions.setLabel: Questions 10–11 refer to the table below.

stimulus.title: CHANGES ON ONE CITY BLOCK IN CITY M, 1880–2025 (HYPOTHETICAL)
columns: Main group living on the block
rows: Lutheran church with a tall steeple; bakery with a German-language name carved in stone over the door
Families of many backgrounds; many German American families move to the suburbs
Bakery building becomes a hardware store; the Lutheran congregation shrinks and later moves away
Church building bought by a Vietnamese Catholic parish; phở restaurants; shop signs in Vietnamese and English
Immigrants from Mexico and Central America, alongside Vietnamese families
Taquería in the former bakery building, under the German name still carved over the door; mural of Our Lady of Guadalupe; shop signs in Spanish; the original church steeple still stands
stimulus.description: A table showing which group mainly lived on one city block during four periods between 1880 and 2025 and the landscape features added in each period. In the latest period, the German name carved over the old bakery door and the original church steeple are still visible.

questions.stem: The changes shown in the table best illustrate

options.A: placelessness
options.B: cultural convergence
options.C: stimulus diffusion
options.D: sequent occupance
options.E: contagious diffusion

rationales.A: Incorrect. Placelessness is the loss of uniqueness in a place's landscape; this block has a distinct, layered landscape.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Cultural convergence is cultures becoming more alike through contact; the table shows a series of groups each adding distinct features.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Stimulus diffusion involves an idea spreading and being changed; the table shows successive groups occupying the same place.
rationales.D: Correct. Sequent occupance is the idea that successive societies leave their cultural imprints on a place, each adding to the cultural landscape. German, Vietnamese, and Mexican and Central American residents each added features, and older features such as the steeple and the carved name remain.
rationales.E: Incorrect. Contagious diffusion is the spread of a trait outward to nearby people and places; the table tracks layers of settlement on one block.

questions.explanation: Sequent occupance means layers. Different groups live in the same place one after another, and each one adds to the landscape. On this block you can still see the German church steeple and the carved bakery name, along with features added later by Vietnamese and then Mexican and Central American residents.

questions.stem: Which concept best describes how the community living on the block shaped its cultural landscape between 1975 and 2005?

options.A: Ethnic neighborhood, because the newcomers' businesses and institutions shaped the space
options.B: Assimilation, because the newcomers gave up their own language and their religion
options.C: Syncretism, because the Lutheran and Catholic traditions blended into a new faith
options.D: Postmodern architecture, because the newcomers built structures that mix many older styles
options.E: Cultural convergence, because the block came to look like city neighborhoods everywhere else

rationales.A: Correct. Residents established a religious institution, restaurants, and signs that reflected their cultural background and served the local community. These features show how ethnicity can shape the use and appearance of space.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The Vietnamese-language signs and the Vietnamese parish show that residents kept their language and their religious community.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The earlier Lutheran congregation and the later Catholic parish are both Christian, and reusing a church building is not the blending of two religions into a new faith.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The table describes reuse of an existing church and new businesses and signs, not a new architectural style.
rationales.E: Incorrect. The features added are distinctive to one group, which makes the block more distinctive, not more like other places.

questions.explanation: When a group settles in one neighborhood, it often builds what it needs: a place of worship, restaurants with familiar food, and signs in its own language. Those choices shape how the space is used and make the block an ethnic neighborhood.

questions.stem: For several generations, residents of a hot, dry region have built houses with thick walls made from local earth, small windows, and flat roofs. Which explanation best accounts for this combination of features?

options.A: Builders copied a colonial power's designs to show loyalty to its rulers.
options.B: Builders adapted nearby materials and designs to the environment.
options.C: Builders mixed decorative details from several past styles to create something new.
options.D: Builders used standard designs promoted by international construction companies.
options.E: Builders reused buildings left by earlier groups but gave them new cultural uses.

rationales.A: Incorrect. The account gives evidence of local materials and environmental conditions, but none of colonial rule or imported designs.
rationales.B: Correct. Traditional architecture adapts to local conditions. Earthen walls slow the movement of heat, small windows limit the sun's heat, and flat roofs are practical where little rain falls.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Mixing details from past styles describes postmodern architecture; the account emphasizes materials and climate, not style.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The account gives no evidence of international companies or standardized global designs.
rationales.E: Incorrect. The account describes a continuing building tradition, not later groups reusing earlier groups' buildings.

questions.explanation: People in hot, dry places have long built with what is nearby and designed homes to fit the weather. Thick earth walls slow the heat, small windows block the sun, and flat roofs work because it rarely rains. Geographers call this traditional architecture: building styles adapted to local materials and climate.

questions.stem: Belgium includes Flanders in the north, where most people speak Dutch, and Wallonia in the south, where most people speak French. Disputes between the two regions have led Belgium's national government to give the regions more control over their own affairs. In this case, language has acted mainly as

options.A: a centrifugal force that divides the state
options.B: a lingua franca that both regions share
options.C: a centripetal force that unites the two regions
options.D: an example of syncretism between two languages
options.E: a result of hierarchical diffusion from Brussels

rationales.A: Correct. A centrifugal force divides a state. Language differences between Dutch-speaking Flanders and French-speaking Wallonia have fueled political disputes and led to the devolution of power to the regions.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Dutch and French are separate languages that dominate different regions, not one shared language.
rationales.C: Incorrect. A centripetal force unites a state; here language differences have fueled disputes between regions.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Syncretism is the blending of traits into a new form; Dutch and French remain distinct languages.
rationales.E: Incorrect. The language divide reflects long-standing regional patterns, not diffusion outward from the capital.

questions.explanation: Centripetal forces pull a country together. Centrifugal forces push it apart. In Belgium, the north and south mostly speak different languages, and arguments between them led the government to give each region more power. Language here pushes the country apart, so it is a centrifugal force.

questions.stem: In parts of southern Louisiana, communities hold festivals featuring Cajun French music and run French immersion programs in public schools. These efforts best illustrate

options.A: assimilation into the dominant national culture
options.B: a centrifugal force weakening national political unity
options.C: placelessness caused by global popular culture
options.D: hierarchical diffusion of French from Paris to Louisiana
options.E: placemaking that builds a regional sense of place

rationales.A: Incorrect. The festivals and language programs support a distinctive regional culture rather than its replacement by the dominant culture.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Celebrating a regional culture does not by itself weaken national unity; nothing in the question describes a movement for separation or self-rule.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Placelessness is the loss of local uniqueness; these efforts make the region more distinctive.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The question describes current local efforts to celebrate and teach a regional language, not the original spread of French to Louisiana.
rationales.E: Correct. Placemaking is the shaping of places to reflect a community's identity. Festivals and language programs strengthen a distinctive regional identity and residents' attachment to the region, showing how language contributes to a sense of place.

questions.explanation: Placemaking means people shaping their places to show who they are. Cajun music festivals and French classes help the region feel special and different from other places. That builds a strong sense of place.

questions.stem: In Country N, most people follow Religion 1, and its shared national festivals strengthen a common identity across regions. In one large city, some residents oppose an immigrant community's plan to build the city's first house of worship for Religion 2. Which statement best describes religion's role in Country N at these two scales?

options.A: Religion is a centrifugal force at the national scale and a centripetal force in the city.
options.B: Religion divides the country at both scales, so the state is likely to break apart.
options.C: The dispute shows that religion no longer shapes identity at the national scale.
options.D: Religion mainly unites the country nationally, but causes tension at the local scale.
options.E: Religion 2 spread to the city by hierarchical diffusion from the national capital.

rationales.A: Incorrect. This reverses the scales: a shared religion unites the country as a whole, and the dispute is local.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The question describes a dispute in one city; nothing suggests the whole state is dividing.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The shared festivals strengthen national identity. A local dispute does not show that religion has become unimportant nationally.
rationales.D: Correct. The shared festivals act as a centripetal force at the national scale. Opposition to the minority community's place of worship creates division at the local scale. A cultural factor can have different effects at different scales.
rationales.E: Incorrect. The scenario describes an immigrant community and gives no evidence that Religion 2 spread from the national capital through hierarchical diffusion.

questions.explanation: Look at the whole country: shared festivals help people feel connected to their country. That is centripetal. Now zoom in to one city: opposition to a minority group's place of worship is causing conflict. That is centrifugal. Religion can work in different ways at different scales.

questions.setLabel: Questions 16–18 refer to the table below.

stimulus.title: FOLLOWERS OF FIVE RELIGIONS, 2025 (HYPOTHETICAL DATA)
columns: Percent of followers living in hearth region
World regions with at least 1 million followers
stimulus.description: A table of five religions showing each religion's hearth region, the percent of its followers who live in that hearth region, the number of world regions with at least 1 million followers, and whether the religion seeks converts.

questions.stem: Which religion in the table shows the pattern most typical of an ethnic religion that has stayed near its hearth?

options.A: Religion P
options.B: Religion Q
options.C: Religion R
options.D: Religion S
options.E: Religion T

rationales.A: Correct. Ethnic religions generally do not seek converts and are usually concentrated near their hearth. Religion P does not seek converts, has 94 percent of its followers in its hearth region, and has at least 1 million followers in only one world region.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Religion Q seeks converts and has at least 1 million followers in six world regions, a pattern typical of a universalizing religion.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Religion R does not seek converts, but more than half of its followers (55 percent) live outside its hearth region, so it has not stayed near its hearth.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Religion S seeks converts and has only 8 percent of its followers in its hearth region.
rationales.E: Incorrect. Religion T is concentrated near its hearth (70 percent), but it seeks converts, a characteristic of universalizing religions.

questions.explanation: Religion P does not seek converts, 94% of its followers live in its hearth region, and it reaches the table's 1-million-follower mark in only one region. Together, these facts best fit an ethnic religion that has stayed near its hearth. That does not mean it has no communities anywhere else.

questions.stem: Based on Religion R's distribution and its approach to seeking converts, which process most plausibly accounts for its presence outside its hearth region?

options.A: Hierarchical diffusion, as rulers adopted it and spread it to their subjects
options.B: Contagious diffusion, as followers converted their neighbors in nearby regions
options.C: Stimulus diffusion, as other religions copied its main beliefs and practices
options.D: Expansion diffusion, as missionaries carried it to new continents
options.E: Relocation diffusion, as followers moved and carried the religion with them

rationales.A: Incorrect. The table provides no evidence that rulers adopted the religion before their subjects. Migration of existing followers is more consistent with the pattern described.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The table does not describe conversion spreading from neighbor to neighbor. Communities outside the hearth can instead result from followers migrating.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Stimulus diffusion would change other religions; it would not place Religion R's own followers outside its hearth.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Missionary work is a way of seeking converts, which Religion R does not do.
rationales.E: Correct. Ethnic religions, which generally do not seek converts, spread mainly through relocation diffusion when their followers migrate, whether by choice or by force. Judaism, whose communities spread through many migrations and expulsions over the centuries, is a real-world example.

questions.explanation: If a religion does not try to win new members, the main way it can show up far away is if its own followers MOVE there. That is relocation diffusion. Judaism is a real example: over many centuries, Jewish communities moved, or were forced to move, to many parts of the world.

questions.stem: Which of the following comparisons CANNOT be made using the data in the table?

options.A: Whether Religion P or Religion R has a higher share of followers living in its hearth region
options.B: Whether Religion Q or Religion S reaches the 1-million-follower threshold in more world regions
options.C: Whether Religion Q or Religion S has more followers worldwide
options.D: Whether Religion Q or Religion T has a higher share of followers living outside its hearth region
options.E: Whether Religion P and Religion R differ in whether they seek converts

rationales.A: Incorrect. The table gives 94 percent for Religion P and 45 percent for Religion R.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Religion Q reaches the threshold in six regions, compared with five for Religion S.
rationales.C: Correct. Counts of regions above a threshold do not give total followers. Each region can have far more than 1 million followers, and smaller groups may live elsewhere.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Subtracting from 100 gives 79 percent outside Religion Q's hearth region and 30 percent outside Religion T's.
rationales.E: Incorrect. The table states that neither Religion P nor Religion R seeks converts.

questions.explanation: The table tells how many regions have at least 1 million followers. It does not tell the total number of followers. One religion could have a few huge communities. Another could have more communities that are just over 1 million. You can read or work out every other comparison from the table.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why Irish, spoken in western Europe, and Bengali, spoken in South Asia, belong to the same language family?

options.A: British colonial rule spread one language to both Ireland and South Asia.
options.B: Both descend from an ancestral language whose speakers spread across Eurasia.
options.C: Both borrowed many of the same words recently through the internet and global media.
options.D: Both developed in similar climates, which produced similar vocabularies.
options.E: Both are creoles that formed when European traders met local populations.

rationales.A: Incorrect. British rule spread English, but Irish and Bengali are separate languages whose relationship is thousands of years older than British colonialism.
rationales.B: Correct. Irish (Celtic branch) and Bengali (Indo-Iranian branch) both descend from Proto-Indo-European. As speakers of that ancestral language and its descendants spread across Europe and South and Southwest Asia, it split into branches and individual languages.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Language families are defined by shared ancestry, not by recent borrowing of words.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Climate does not produce related languages; relationships come from a common ancestral language.
rationales.E: Incorrect. Neither language is a creole; both are long-established languages with deep histories in their regions.

questions.explanation: A language family is like a family tree. Irish and Bengali are very distant cousins. Both come from one very old language, Proto-Indo-European. As its speakers spread out over thousands of years, it split into many branches, like Celtic in the west and Indo-Iranian in the east.

questions.stem: Buddhism and Hinduism both began in South Asia. Today most Buddhists live in East and Southeast Asia, while most Hindus still live in South Asia. Which of the following best explains this difference?

options.A: Buddhist missionaries and traders spread it widely; Hinduism is an ethnic religion.
options.B: Hinduism began more recently than Buddhism, so it has had less time to spread.
options.C: The climate of East Asia was better suited to Buddhist practices than South Asia's.
options.D: Buddhism is an ethnic religion tied to the peoples of East and Southeast Asia.
options.E: Buddhism spread mainly as large numbers of farmers from South Asia migrated east.

rationales.A: Correct. Buddhism is a universalizing religion: monks, missionaries, and traders carried it along overland and sea routes to Central, East, and Southeast Asia, and some rulers adopted and promoted it. Hinduism is an ethnic religion that does not generally seek converts, so most Hindus still live near its hearth in South Asia.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Hinduism's roots are older than Buddhism, which began about 2,500 years ago.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Climate does not explain the spread of a belief system; the difference reflects how each religion relates to converts.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Buddhism is a universalizing religion; it began in South Asia and spread to East and Southeast Asia.
rationales.E: Incorrect. Buddhism spread mainly through missionaries, traders, and the support of rulers, not through mass migration of farmers.

questions.explanation: Buddhism is a universalizing religion. Monks, traders, and rulers carried it from South Asia along trade routes, and many people converted. Hinduism is an ethnic religion, and most Hindus still live in South Asia. Hindu traditions did spread long ago to parts of Southeast Asia, and Hindu communities now live around the world.

questions.setLabel: Questions 21–22 refer to the graph and information below.

stimulus.title: SHARE OF PEOPLE WHO SPEAK ORVANI AT HOME, BY AGE GROUP, COUNTRY K, 1995 AND 2025 (HYPOTHETICAL DATA)
stimulus.yLabel: Percent who speak Orvani at home
stimulus.text: Orvani is an Indigenous language spoken mainly in rural areas of Country K. Since 1995, many young people have moved to Country K's cities, where schools and most jobs use the national language and much online content is in English. In 2023, a group of young Orvani speakers launched a popular Orvani-language music channel and video series online.
stimulus.description: Grouped bar chart of the percent of people in each age group who speak Orvani at home in 1995 and 2025. Ages 10–19: 48 and 12. Ages 20–39: 60 and 30. Ages 40–59: 72 and 52. Ages 60 and over: 85 and 70.

questions.stem: Which conclusion is best supported by the graph?

options.A: Orvani use fell more among older people than among younger people.
options.B: In 2025, a majority of people ages 20–39 spoke Orvani at home.
options.C: Orvani use fell by the same number of percentage points in every age group.
options.D: Older people were less likely than younger people to speak Orvani at home in 2025.
options.E: Orvani use fell in every age group, and the steepest drop was among the youngest.

rationales.A: Incorrect. The youngest group fell the most (36 percentage points, from 48 to 12 percent), while people 60 and over fell the least (15 points).
rationales.B: Incorrect. In 2025, 30 percent of people ages 20–39 spoke Orvani at home, less than half.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The declines were 36, 30, 20, and 15 percentage points, so they were not equal.
rationales.D: Incorrect. In 2025, 70 percent of people 60 and over spoke Orvani at home, compared with 12 percent of people ages 10–19.
rationales.E: Correct. The share speaking Orvani at home declined in all four age groups. The largest decline was 36 percentage points among people ages 10–19, from 48 percent to 12 percent.

questions.explanation: Compare each pair of bars. Every age group had a lower share using Orvani at home in 2025. The largest drop was among ages 10–19: 48 minus 12 equals 36 percentage points. The bars compare age groups in two different years, not the same people. They also do not show how well people speak Orvani in other settings.

questions.stem: The online Orvani-language music channel described in the information best illustrates which of the following?

options.A: Relocation diffusion carried Orvani from the cities back out to rural villages.
options.B: Online media can spread English worldwide, so the channel is an example of cultural convergence.
options.C: Urbanization reversed the decline in Orvani use among young people by 2025.
options.D: Online media can promote cultural divergence by helping a minority language stay distinct.
options.E: Assimilation, because young Orvani speakers adopted the national culture online.

rationales.A: Incorrect. The information describes an online channel, not people moving from cities to villages.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The channel uses Orvani and can support its continued use. Using a global technology does not, by itself, show cultural convergence.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The information links moving to cities with less use of Orvani, not more, and the chart has no measurement between 1995 and 2025, so it cannot show a reversal after the channel began.
rationales.D: Correct. The AP course framework notes that communication technologies such as the internet can create both cultural convergence and cultural divergence. An Orvani-language channel uses global technology to keep a minority language distinct, an example of cultural divergence.
rationales.E: Incorrect. Creating content in their own minority language is the opposite of giving up that language for the national culture.

questions.explanation: Online media can spread widely used languages like English. But they can also help people keep minority languages alive. The channel gives people new chances to use and share Orvani. It can help keep cultures different even when everyone uses the same technology. Geographers call this kind of change cultural divergence.

questions.stem: In the mid-1800s, before the first lasting telegraph cable crossed the Atlantic Ocean in 1866, news traveled between Europe and North America by ship and took more than a week to arrive. Today, a video posted in London can be watched in New York seconds later. This change best illustrates

options.A: distance decay
options.B: stimulus diffusion
options.C: time-space convergence
options.D: relocation diffusion
options.E: hierarchical diffusion

rationales.A: Incorrect. Distance decay is the decline in interaction as distance increases; the question describes the time needed to connect two places shrinking.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Stimulus diffusion is the spread of an idea that is changed by the culture receiving it.
rationales.C: Correct. Time-space convergence is the reduction in the time it takes for people, goods, or information to travel between places because of improvements in transportation and communication technology.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Relocation diffusion involves people moving and carrying culture with them; the video spreads without anyone moving.
rationales.E: Incorrect. Hierarchical diffusion moves from more important people or places to less important ones; the question is about how fast information travels.

questions.explanation: Time-space convergence means places feel closer together because it takes less time to reach them. News that once took more than a week by ship now arrives in seconds. London and New York did not move, but in travel time they got much closer.

questions.stem: Santería, a religion that developed in Cuba, honors spirits called orichas that come from the Yoruba religion of West Africa. Enslaved Yoruba people brought this religion to the island. Many orichas are identified with Roman Catholic saints introduced under Spanish colonial rule. Santería best illustrates

options.A: assimilation, because the Yoruba traditions disappeared into Catholicism
options.B: syncretism, because elements of two religions blended into a new form
options.C: multiculturalism, because the two religions stayed separate side by side
options.D: ethnocentrism, because one group judged the other's religion as inferior
options.E: contagious diffusion, because Santería spread from Cuba to nearby islands

rationales.A: Incorrect. Yoruba traditions did not disappear; they remain central to Santería.
rationales.B: Correct. Syncretism is the blending of elements from different cultures, such as religious beliefs and practices, into a new cultural form. Santería combines Yoruba religious traditions with elements of Roman Catholicism.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Multiculturalism describes distinct cultures coexisting while keeping their identities; in Santería, the traditions merged.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Ethnocentrism is an attitude of judging other cultures by one's own standards; it does not describe the blending of religions.
rationales.E: Incorrect. The question describes how Santería formed, not how it spread to other places.

questions.explanation: Syncretism means blending. Santería took parts of Yoruba religion from West Africa and parts of Catholicism from Spain and merged them into something new. Both traditions are still visible inside it.

questions.stem: In 1971, Canada adopted an official national policy of multiculturalism. The policy supports the freedom of immigrants and other groups to keep their languages, religions, and traditions while taking part in Canadian society. Which change in the cultural landscape would this policy most likely encourage?

options.A: Official government signs switching from English and French to immigrants' heritage languages
options.B: Immigrant families being required to settle outside ethnic neighborhoods so that groups mix evenly
options.C: New houses of worship that blend the country's religions into one shared faith
options.D: Cultural centers and festivals of many groups staying visible in shared public spaces
options.E: Identical shopping malls and chain stores replacing regional and ethnic differences

rationales.A: Incorrect. Canada's policy was set within a framework of two official languages, English and French. It supports groups' freedom to keep heritage languages but does not replace the official languages.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The policy supports freedom to keep traditions; it does not decide where people live, and ethnic neighborhoods remain common in Canadian cities.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Blending religions into one faith describes syncretism; the policy supports groups' freedom to keep their own religions.
rationales.D: Correct. Multiculturalism supports many cultural groups keeping their traditions within one society, so the landscape would keep showing distinct cultural centers and festivals alongside shared public spaces and institutions.
rationales.E: Incorrect. Look-alike chain landscapes reflect placelessness and cultural convergence, not a policy that supports cultural distinctiveness.

questions.explanation: Multiculturalism supports people's freedom to keep their traditions while taking part in one shared society. On the landscape, you would see cultural centers, places of worship, and festivals of many groups. You would also see schools, parks, and other public places that everyone shares.
